questions.question_text: Write $5\text{ kg }300\text{ g}$ as a decimal number of kilograms.

options.why: Places 300 grams in the hundredths position instead of writing 0.3 kilogram.
Treats 300 grams as 3 grams when forming the decimal part.
Uses grams as the final unit while retaining a kilogram-sized decimal value.

questions.question_text: Write $9\text{ kg }45\text{ g}$ as a decimal number of kilograms.

options.why: Treats 45 grams as 45 hundredths rather than 45 thousandths of a kilogram.
Introduces an extra zero and makes 45 grams ten times too small.
Places the digits 4 and 5 in the tenths and thousandths positions, inserting zero in the wrong place.

questions.question_text: Write $7.208\text{ kg}$ as kilograms and grams.

options.why: Drops the zero that holds the tens-of-grams place.
Multiplies the decimal part by 100 instead of 1000.
Reverses the final two place-value digits in the gram amount.

questions.question_text: Which mass is equal to $0.064\text{ kg}$?

options.why: Moves the decimal only two places instead of multiplying kilograms by 1000.
Moves the decimal four places and makes the mass ten times too large.
Changes the unit label without converting the numerical value.

questions.question_text:
A scale shows $3.09\text{ kg}$.
Which mixed-unit label is equivalent?

options.why: Treats nine hundredths of a kilogram as nine grams instead of ninety grams.
Treats 0.09 kilogram as 0.9 kilogram, making the gram part ten times too large.
Treats the decimal digits as whole kilograms worth of grams.
Writes the gram digits straight after the decimal point, so sixty grams becomes six tenths of a kilogram instead of $0.06\text{ kg}$.
Pads with one zero too many, making sixty grams ten times too small in decimal kilograms.
Pads with an extra zero, making six hundred grams ten times too small; $600\text{ g}=0.6\text{ kg}$.
